title: Dissipation-enhanced scrambling in the SYK model coupled to a lossy cavity
authors: Pietro Pelliconi, Bastien Lapierre, Shinsei Ryu
abstract: We study the Yukawa-Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, a disordered model of $N$ Majorana fermions and $R=γN$ bosons in which the bosons are linearly coupled to independent realizations of SYK $p$-body interactions, in the presence of dissipation, modeled by a Lindblad master equation. Motivated by recent proposals for implementing SYK models in quantum simulators, we focus on bosonic leakage at rate $κ$. Initializing the system in the steady state, we analyze the late-time fermionic relaxation rate and the Lyapunov exponent, solving the large-$N$ theory both numerically and for $p$ large, finding a rich landscape of dynamical behaviors. Most notably, the Lyapunov exponent remains positive for every value of $κ$ and, for $p>2$, can even grow as $κ$ increases. The QED case $p=2$, which lies between the fully chaotic regime $p>2$ and the integrable case $p=1$, exhibits special features. We also identify a critical value of the boson-to-fermion ratio $γ_c \approx 2/p^2$ separating distinct dynamical regimes.
summary: This work analyzes the SYK model coupled to a dissipative cavity environment to study quantum scrambling. By solving the dynamics in the large-$N$ limit, the authors find that dissipation does not destroy chaos; instead, it can enhance the scrambling rate, quantified by the Lyapunov exponent. This suggests that coupling to a lossy bath can be a source of enhanced quantum chaos.
main_problem: The study investigates how dissipation, modeled by bosonic leakage, affects quantum information scrambling in the SYK model.
main_result: The Lyapunov exponent remains positive for all dissipation rates, and for $p>2$, it can even increase as the leakage rate $\kappa$ increases, indicating dissipation-enhanced scrambling.
method: The analysis employs the large-$N$ limit, solving the Lindblad master equation via the Schwinger-Keldysh path integral and deriving equations of motion for fluctuations.
model_or_system: The system is the Yukawa-Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (YSYK) model, comprising Majorana fermions and bosons, coupled to a lossy cavity environment modeled by a Lindblad master equation.
key_observables: Late-time fermionic relaxation rate ($\Gamma$) and the Lyapunov exponent ($\lambda$), which diagnoses chaotic dynamics.
important_parameters: The interaction order $p$, the boson-to-fermion ratio $\gamma$, and the bosonic leakage rate $\kappa$. A critical ratio $\gamma_c = 2/p^2$ is identified.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes Markovian dissipation described by the Lindblad equation and utilizes the large-$N$ limit and auxiliary boson approximations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 sketches a realization in cQED platforms and shows that the Lyapunov exponent ($\lambda$) remains positive and is enhanced at finite $\kappa$ for $p > 2$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by setting up the YSYK model with dissipation, deriving the effective action via path integrals, calculating the ladder kernels for OTOCs, and finally solving the resulting ODE to determine the Lyapunov exponent's dependence on dissipation.
why_interesting: The explicit inclusion of dissipation ($\kappa$) into the calculation of chaos measures like the Lyapunov exponent, showing enhancement rather than suppression, is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 1. We study the dissipative dynamics of the p–body YSYK model in the presence of bosonic leakage κ. (a) Sketch of a possible realization in cQED platforms, where bosonic interactions are mediated by dispersive bosons, which can also leak out of the cavity. (b) Sketch of the dissipation–enhanced scrambling: the Lyapunov exponent λ stays positive for any p and any leakage strength κ, and is enhanced at finite κ for p > 2.

Figure 2. Late time relaxation rate Γ for p = 2. The dots have been obtained solving numerically the Schwinger– Dyson equations (20–29) choosing ∆= 1 and J = 0.05. For this choice of parameters the auxiliary approximation hold. We then compare the large–p result (54), finding remarkable agreement.

Figure 3. a) Dissipative Lyapunov exponent for p = 2, computed numerically. The case p = 2 is the QED vertex, thus is the most relevant for platforms such as cavity–QED and circuit–QED. As predicted by the large–p result, the Lyapunov exponent is always positive, it is monotonically decreasing in κ, and for large dissipation it becomes independent of γ, decaying as κ−3. b) Dissipative Lyapunov exponent for γ = 1 and different values of p, compared to the large–p auxiliary result. For p = 2, λ is monotonically decreasing and highly suppressed at large κ. For p > 2 and γ > 2/p2, scrambling is enhanced until κ = κ∗as in (93), and then decreases as ∼κ−1.
